title: Using Projects for work

body.text: Projects are ideal for repetitive work or work that needs consistency. Real examples: a
Project for writing blog or social media content
with the brand voice and style guide in its Knowledge, or a customer support Project where Claude answers questions following set FAQs and company policy — so
everyone on the team gets output to the same standard

example: "This Project already has all the product info. Draft a reply for a customer asking about the return policy — polite and concise."

title: Real-world Project examples

body.text: Beyond content and support, Projects also suit
— like a language-learning Project where Claude knows your level and picks up where you left off, or a project-management Project with your team info and timeline. Having separate Projects means you
don't mix the contexts of different kinds of work
, so Claude stays focused and more accurate.

example: "My Japanese-learning Project: I've studied for 3 months and know all of Hiragana and Katakana. Today I want to practice 10 basic Kanji."

question: What's the benefit of separating Projects by type of work?

options.text: It prevents mixing contexts, so Claude stays focused and more accurate

question: Which kind of Project is best suited to Claude Projects?

options.text: A one-time question you never use again
A blog-writing Project that needs a consistent style and brand voice

question: To have Claude help manage a team, what should you put in Project Knowledge?

options.text: Team info, timeline, and work rules

question: To have Claude help with HR work consistently, what should you put in Project Knowledge?

options.text: Company policies, document templates, and relevant regulations

question: What's the benefit of separating Projects by type of work?

options.text: Contexts don't mix, so answers fit each area of work
